variants.title: Follow one token
variants.context: An MoE layer is a distributed join over one token. The router scores experts, top-K selection admits destinations against per-expert capacity, dispatch moves representations to the devices owning those weights, the selected experts run, and combine restores token order and applies the router weights before the residual continues.
variants.prompt: A single token enters a top-2 MoE layer on a healthy fleet. Put the stages in order.

items.text: Run only the selected feed-forward networks while recording overflow, queueing, and device failures.
Combine by returning results to token order and applying the router weights before the residual connection.
Dispatch by grouping token representations per expert and moving them to the devices owning those weights.
Score experts by projecting the token representation into one score per expert and ranking them.
Select top-K destinations and check each one against its per-batch capacity.

variants.hint: The router is a learned model component, not an external load balancer.
variants.explanation: Every admitted token must reach its intended experts within capacity and return one correctly weighted result, which is what the combine stage restores.

variants.title: Follow one token
variants.context: An MoE layer is a distributed join over one token. The router scores experts, top-K selection admits destinations against per-expert capacity, dispatch moves representations to the devices owning those weights, the selected experts run, and combine restores token order and applies the router weights before the residual continues.
variants.prompt: A token selects an expert that is already at capacity for this batch. Put the stages in order, ending with what the residual path receives.

items.text: Admission compares the selected destination against that expert's remaining capacity for the batch.
The router produces scores and combination weights for the token.
Combine applies the router weights to whatever contributions exist and reconnects the residual path.
The overflowing assignment is resolved by the declared policy: drop, reroute, queue, or fall back.
The experts that did admit the token execute and record the overflow event.

variants.hint: Capacity is checked at admission, before anything crosses the network.
variants.explanation: Overflow is decided at admission, so the declared policy determines what the residual path receives rather than leaving it undefined.

variants.title: Follow one token
variants.context: An MoE layer is a distributed join over one token. The router scores experts, top-K selection admits destinations against per-expert capacity, dispatch moves representations to the devices owning those weights, the selected experts run, and combine restores token order and applies the router weights before the residual continues.
variants.prompt: An expert-owning device fails while the router is still selecting its experts. Put the stages in order.

items.text: Combine validates coverage so every admitted token still returns a weighted result.
Admission tries to place assignments on the failed owner's experts.
The router scores experts without knowing that one owner is unavailable.
Dispatch surfaces the unreachable destination instead of silently hanging on it.
The degraded path runs: a replica, a compatible reroute, or the trained fallback executes.

variants.hint: Availability means bounded behavior, not the absence of failure.
variants.explanation: Raising the capacity factor does not make failed expert weights reachable, so replicas, reroutes, or a fallback carry the token instead.

variants.title: Gate the MoE release
variants.context: An MoE release is gated on failure behavior, not only on quality. Routing traces are replayed, quality and overflow and dispatch tails are compared on production slices, an expert owner is removed to prove degraded semantics, and router and expert weights are canaried together.
variants.prompt: A new router and new expert weights are ready. Put the release gates in order.

items.text: Compare quality, overflow, all-to-all volume, and tails across production token slices.
Replay representative routing traces against the candidate router and placement plan.
Roll back on quality slices, dropped-token rate, expert imbalance, dispatch p99, or degraded-mode failure.
Remove one expert owner and verify rerouting, replica, or fallback semantics under load.
Canary router and expert-weight versions together, rejecting mixed versions unless compatibility is explicit.

variants.hint: The degraded mode is tested before it is needed, not after.
variants.explanation: Routing is a model decision and a systems constraint at once, so the gate covers quality, overflow, communication tails, and failure behavior together.

variants.title: Gate the MoE release
variants.context: An MoE release is gated on failure behavior, not only on quality. Routing traces are replayed, quality and overflow and dispatch tails are compared on production slices, an expert owner is removed to prove degraded semantics, and router and expert weights are canaried together.
variants.prompt: A candidate adds 32 experts and the team wants evidence before scaling the topology. Put the validation steps in order.

items.text: Validate one topology end to end, including fault domains and checkpoint ownership.
Pilot the change in selected feed-forward layers while keeping shared or dense fallback paths.
Replay real token traces so routing concentration is measured on production slices rather than an average batch.
Compare quality, active FLOPs, resident memory, dispatch volume, and p99 against a tuned dense baseline.
Scale expert count only after that topology holds its quality and tail evidence.

variants.hint: The question is the measured quality-cost frontier, not the parameter count.
variants.explanation: A hybrid pilot bounds the blast radius, and one validated topology is the prerequisite for adding expert capacity.

variants.title: Gate the MoE release
variants.context: An MoE release is gated on failure behavior, not only on quality. Routing traces are replayed, quality and overflow and dispatch tails are compared on production slices, an expert owner is removed to prove degraded semantics, and router and expert weights are canaried together.
variants.prompt: Dispatch p99 regressed on one network cut after a placement change. Put the response in order.

items.text: Change the placement plan so the expert-parallel group stops crossing the saturated link.
Inspect dispatch bytes, queue time, collective duration, and source-destination skew on the affected cut.
Separate the stages with layer-level evidence for routing, fabric, and expert health.
Re-measure the same token slices before promoting the placement further.
Confirm expert assignment counts are balanced so routing is ruled out as the cause.

variants.hint: End-to-end latency alone cannot say which stage failed.
variants.explanation: One universal tuning change usually moves the bottleneck, so the failed stage is identified from layer-level telemetry before anything is adjusted.

variants.title: Choose the routing contract
variants.context: Routing contracts differ in who chooses. Token choice lets each token pick its top experts, switch routing picks exactly one, expert choice lets each expert take tokens up to a fixed capacity, and deterministic routing assigns by hash or rule with no learned specialization.
variants.prompt: A serving team needs per-expert load bounded by construction so no hot expert can overflow a batch. Which contract fits?
options: Expert choice, letting each expert take tokens up to a fixed capacity.
Switch routing, letting each token select exactly one expert.
Token choice, letting each token select its highest-scoring experts.
optionFeedback: Correct: expert choice bounds load by construction, though token coverage and combination semantics then need validation.
Top-1 shrinks dispatch volume but does nothing to stop many tokens choosing the same expert.
Token choice is exactly the contract where hot experts must be contained by capacity controls.
variants.hint: Ask which side of the assignment gets to decide.
variants.explanation: Expert choice bounds load by construction because intake is capped per expert, which moves the open question to whether every token was covered.

variants.title: Choose the routing contract
variants.context: Routing contracts differ in who chooses. Token choice lets each token pick its top experts, switch routing picks exactly one, expert choice lets each expert take tokens up to a fixed capacity, and deterministic routing assigns by hash or rule with no learned specialization.
variants.prompt: An operations team wants assignments that are reproducible from the token alone and is not trying to learn semantic specialization. Which contract fits?
options: Token choice, because top-K scores are recomputed the same way each time.
Expert choice, because a fixed capacity makes intake predictable.
Deterministic routing by hash or rule, which is reproducible and operationally simple.
optionFeedback: A learned router's assignments move with checkpoints, precision, and batch shape.
Bounded intake does not make a specific token's destination reproducible.
Correct: hash or rule assignment is reproducible, at the cost of no learned specialization.
variants.hint: Reproducibility and learned specialization pull in opposite directions here.
variants.explanation: Deterministic routing trades the model's ability to learn specialization for assignments that can be reproduced and reasoned about operationally.

variants.title: Choose the routing contract
variants.context: Routing contracts differ in who chooses. Token choice lets each token pick its top experts, switch routing picks exactly one, expert choice lets each expert take tokens up to a fixed capacity, and deterministic routing assigns by hash or rule with no learned specialization.
variants.prompt: A team is dispatch-bandwidth bound and willing to accept that a token has no second selected path. Which contract fits?
options: Deterministic routing, since rules avoid the router's dispatch entirely.
Switch routing, since top-1 halves expert assignments relative to top-2.
Expert choice, since bounded intake reduces the bytes that move.
optionFeedback: Rule-based assignment still moves the same token vectors to the owning devices.
Correct: top-1 executes one expert per token, so assignments and dispatch volume drop against top-2.
Bounded intake caps per-expert work but does not shrink the assignments a token generates.
variants.hint: Count how many assignments each token creates.
variants.explanation: Top-2 roughly doubles assignments and dispatch volume for the same batch, so top-1 is the contract that directly reduces both.

variants.title: Define the overflow semantics
variants.context: Overflow semantics are part of correctness. Dropping is bounded but leaves the residual path with no expert contribution, rerouting preserves work while changing semantics, queueing preserves the chosen expert but lets one hot expert set batch tail latency, and a fallback must be trained and evaluated as a real degraded mode.
variants.prompt: Match each overflow policy to the cost it imposes.

pairs.label: Drop
pairs.detail: Fast and bounded, but the residual path gets no expert contribution.

pairs.label: Reroute
pairs.detail: Preserves the work, but changes model semantics and adds latency.

pairs.label: Queue
pairs.detail: Preserves the chosen expert, but one hot expert sets batch tail latency.

pairs.label: Fallback
pairs.detail: Keeps a contribution, but only if the degraded path was trained and evaluated.

variants.hint: Each policy protects something different: latency, work, choice, or coverage.
variants.explanation: Overflow behavior is part of correctness, so the policy is chosen deliberately and evaluated rather than inherited from a framework default.

variants.title: Define the overflow semantics
variants.context: Overflow semantics are part of correctness. Dropping is bounded but leaves the residual path with no expert contribution, rerouting preserves work while changing semantics, queueing preserves the chosen expert but lets one hot expert set batch tail latency, and a fallback must be trained and evaluated as a real degraded mode.
variants.prompt: Match each requirement to the overflow policy it points to.

pairs.label: Every token must keep some expert contribution
pairs.detail: Route it to a shared or dense path that was trained for this.

pairs.label: Batch latency must stay bounded above all else
pairs.detail: Discard the excess assignment and record it.

pairs.label: A compatible expert with spare capacity exists
pairs.detail: Send the assignment there and accept the semantic change.

pairs.label: The selected expert specifically must run this token
pairs.detail: Make the assignment wait for that expert's turn.

variants.hint: Start from what the requirement refuses to give up.
variants.explanation: The requirement selects the policy, because no single overflow behavior preserves latency, work, expert choice, and coverage at once.

variants.title: Define the overflow semantics
variants.context: Overflow semantics are part of correctness. Dropping is bounded but leaves the residual path with no expert contribution, rerouting preserves work while changing semantics, queueing preserves the chosen expert but lets one hot expert set batch tail latency, and a fallback must be trained and evaluated as a real degraded mode.
variants.prompt: Match each observed symptom to the overflow policy that explains it.

pairs.label: Batch tail latency tracks the busiest expert
pairs.detail: Assignments are waiting for their selected expert.

pairs.label: Quality falls on one token slice while latency stays flat
pairs.detail: Excess assignments are being discarded silently.

pairs.label: Outputs shift whenever a neighbor expert has spare room
pairs.detail: Assignments are being sent to a different expert.

pairs.label: A degraded path runs in production but was never evaluated
pairs.detail: An untested shared or dense route is absorbing the excess.

variants.hint: Ask which resource the symptom spends: time, quality, or semantics.
variants.explanation: Overflow policies leave different fingerprints in telemetry, which is why drop, reroute, and queue rates are tracked per layer and token slice.

variants.title: Do the capacity math
variants.context: Capacity planning uses simple arithmetic over T tokens, K experts per token, E experts, and capacity factor C. Total assignments are T times K, balanced assignments per expert are T times K divided by E, and capacity per expert is that balanced figure scaled by C. Anything above capacity must drop, reroute, wait, or fall back.
variants.prompt: A batch has 8,192 tokens with top-2 routing across 16 experts. If load were perfectly balanced, how many assignments would each expert receive?
variants.hint: Count the assignments the batch creates before dividing them up.
variants.explanation: Balanced assignments per expert are T times K divided by E, so top-2 routing over 8,192 tokens creates 16,384 assignments spread across 16 experts.

mistakes.feedback: That divides tokens by experts and forgets that top-2 routing creates two assignments per token.
That is the total number of assignments in the batch, not the share per expert.

variants.title: Do the capacity math
variants.context: Capacity planning uses simple arithmetic over T tokens, K experts per token, E experts, and capacity factor C. Total assignments are T times K, balanced assignments per expert are T times K divided by E, and capacity per expert is that balanced figure scaled by C. Anything above capacity must drop, reroute, wait, or fall back.
variants.prompt: A batch has 4,096 tokens, switch routing with one expert per token, 8 experts, and a capacity factor of 1.5. What is the planned capacity per expert?
variants.hint: The capacity factor scales the balanced share, not the whole batch.
variants.explanation: Capacity per expert is the capacity factor times T times K divided by E, which reserves headroom above the balanced share for uneven routing.

mistakes.feedback: That is the balanced share with the capacity factor left out.
That scales the whole batch by the factor without dividing across the experts.

variants.title: Do the capacity math
variants.context: Capacity planning uses simple arithmetic over T tokens, K experts per token, E experts, and capacity factor C. Total assignments are T times K, balanced assignments per expert are T times K divided by E, and capacity per expert is that balanced figure scaled by C. Anything above capacity must drop, reroute, wait, or fall back.
variants.prompt: Capacity is 1,024 assignments per expert for this batch. Measured routing sends 1,300 assignments to one hot expert. How many assignments must drop, reroute, wait, or fall back?
variants.hint: Overflow is what the expert cannot admit, not what it received.
variants.explanation: Overflow is the assignments above capacity, and a measured hot-expert multiplier is why planning cannot stop at the balanced average.

mistakes.feedback: That is everything the expert was sent, not the part above capacity.
That is the capacity itself; the overflow is the excess over it.
